chapterTitle: Chord and Arcs of a Circle
explanation: Theorem 9.1 states one and only one circle can pass through three non-collinear points.
stem: Through how many circles can three non-collinear points A, B and C lie?

chapterTitle: Chord and Arcs of a Circle
explanation: Theorem 9.2: a line from the centre that bisects a chord is perpendicular to that chord.

chapterTitle: Chord and Arcs of a Circle
explanation: Theorem 9.3: a perpendicular from the centre onto a chord bisects that chord, so AC = BC.
options: [{"key":"A","text":"AC and BC are unrelated"},{"key":"C","text":"AC is always greater than BC"},{"key":"B","text":"AC = BC, so C bisects AB"},{"key":"D","text":"C lies outside the chord"}]

chapterTitle: Chord and Arcs of a Circle
explanation: Theorem 9.4: congruent chords of a circle are equidistant from the centre.
options: [{"key":"A","text":"They must be equal"},{"key":"B","text":"AB is always closer to O"},{"key":"C","text":"CD is always closer to O"},{"key":"D","text":"No relationship is guaranteed"}]
stem: Chords AB and CD of a circle are equal in length. What does Theorem 9.4 say about their perpendicular distances from the centre O?

chapterTitle: Chord and Arcs of a Circle
explanation: Theorem 9.5: chords of a circle equidistant from the centre are congruent (equal in length).
options: [{"key":"A","text":"PQ and RS must be equal in length"},{"key":"B","text":"PQ must be longer than RS"},{"key":"C","text":"PQ and RS must be perpendicular"},{"key":"D","text":"Nothing can be concluded"}]
